newsitem.title: ANTARCTICA: FEATURE-People and penguins feel Antarctic warming.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-People and penguins feel Antarctic warming.

text.p: Adelie penquins used to crowd this island so thickly you would think you had wandered into a headwaiters convention, but global warming has sent many of them searching for colder climes.

The temperature is a balmy 50 degrees (10 C), the sun shines and U.S. scientist Bill Fraser wears a light jacket as he strides across bare ground to show a visitor what is left. "This area used to be covered in Adelie nests. You can see where they used to be, where there are lots of pebbles."

Adelie penguins still breed on craggy Cormorant Island, but not in the numbers they used to, and Fraser and other scientists see the decline as just one effect of climate change in the Antarctica Peninsula. Receding glaciers, milder winters, dramatic changes in seal and penguin populations -- they are all signs that the warming of Antarctica, once a vague prediction by researchers, is now a reality.

Most of the changes are still subtle. But nowhere are they more apparent than on the rocky islets around the U.S. National Science Foundation's Palmer Station, an area teeming with seals, penguins, petrels and skuas. It is a place of dazzling beauty, where weirdly shaped icebergs float past with penguins perched on the edge, pieces of glaciers collapse into the ocean and Weddell seals doze on rocks.
The ocean varies from cold dark blue to a tropical-looking turquoise, the occasional whale spouts up from the sea, and the sun sets at 2 a.m. only to rise again an hour later.
BABY, IT USED TO BE COLD OUTSIDE

On an unusually warm day like this, you can almost forget that Antarctica is rightly called "the frozen continent." Heat-stressed penguins are panting or sliding down snowbanks to try to cool off. Elephant seals bask in the sun in fetid pools. There may still be debate about why the Antarctic climate is changing -- because of man's greenhouse gases, a natural cyclical upswing or some combination -- but there is no doubt it is changing. The mean temperature on the Antarctic Peninsula has risen by about two degrees (one degree celsius) since 1950.

"There's some dispute about the causes of changes in species populations. But the peninsula is melting, I don't think there's any question about that anymore," said Fraser, a Montana State University ecologist and chief scientist at Palmer Station.

Worldwide, 1995 was the warmest year on record. Last year was slightly cooler but still well above the average since 1961, indicating that global warming is happening, the British Meteorological Society said.

About 140 countries have ratified the 1992 Climate Change Convention committing them to stabilising emissions of gases believed to cause global warming, a phenomenon linked to changes in weather patterns, rising sea levels and disruption in weather patterns.

In Antarctica, climate change is being felt in unexpected ways. Winter pack ice, which in extremely cold winters can cover the ocean almost half way across the Drake Passage to South America, is tending to cover less and less area.

In the 1950s, about four out of five winters saw extensive seasonal pack ice, according to various studies using NASA satellite data. Now the rate is one or two out of every five years and that change is having a crucial effect on the way wildlife reproduces, scientists say. Among penguins, species like the Adelie that rely on pack ice are posting population declines, while those like the Chinstrap penguin that shun pack ice and prefer open seas are increasing in number.

Heavier snow, also possibly due to warming, seems to be cutting into some penguin populations because the snow covers their nesting sites longer into the spring breeding season. At the same time, more northerly, warmer-water species like the Rockhopper and Magellanic penguins are becoming more common in the southern limits of their range, Fraser said.

Among seals, similar changes are occurring. Weddell and Crabeater seals, which like the Adelie penguin depend on pack ice, are declining, while species such as the elephant seal and especially the fur seal that avoid pack ice are increasing. Almost exterminated by hunters in the 1800s, fur seals have multiplied in the South Georgia Islands to levels exceeding those before they were hunted, British studies show.

The continent's few hardy plant species simply shut down in warm air. "Corn and soybeans love it but if you increase the air temperature to 12 degrees C (53.6 F) or 15 degrees C (59 F), these plants die," Arizona State University botanist Xiong Fusheng said.

A vast glacier covering Anvers Island, where Palmer Station is located, has receded over 20 years, leaving in its wake new islands being gradually colonised by seabirds and seals. "Retreat of glaciers seems to be happening all over the west coast of the peninsula," Fraser said.

Glacial movements take years to reveal patterns. Wildlife populations will also take years of study before definitive conclusions are possible, and scientists do not yet fully understand the effects of naturally occurring cyclical changes on climate and sea ice. Researchers are also careful not to shoehorn all changes into the context of global warming.

But studies by David Karl of the University of Hawaii and others suggest links between the extent of Antarctic sea ice and El Nino, the warm ocean current that pounds the coasts of Ecuador and Peru with rain every six or seven years.
